present.name: Present-tense endings
present.about: The verb's ending changes with who does it, so Portuguese often leaves eu out: (eu) falo (I speak), você fala (you speak), a gente fala (we speak).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

present.short: The verb's ending says who: eu tomo, você toma, nós tomamos (I drink, you drink, we drink).

gender.name: Gender and agreement
gender.about: Every noun is masculine or feminine, and o or a, um or uma and the adjectives with it match it: o carro novo, a casa nova, as casas novas.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gender.short: Every noun is an o word or an a word, and um or uma and its adjectives match: o celular, a mesa, um café, uma água.

possessive.name: meu, minha: my
possessive.about: meu or minha, seu or sua match the thing owned, not the owner, and Brazilians often put o or a before them: minha irmã (my sister), o meu celular (the my phone).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

possessive.short: meu goes with an o word and minha with an a word: meu celular, minha chave (my phone, my key).

adjective-after.name: Adjectives after the noun
adjective-after.about: Most describing words come after the noun: uma casa amarela (a house yellow).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

adjective-after.short: Most adjectives come after the noun: uma casa amarela (a house yellow); a few like bom come before or after.

negation.name: não before the verb
negation.about: não comes before the verb and any little pronoun in front of it: Eu não sei (I not know), Eu não me lembro (I not myself remember).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

negation.short: não goes right before the verb: Eu não tomo café (I not drink coffee: I don't drink coffee).

question.name: Questions
question.about: A question usually keeps the order of a statement: Você fala inglês? (you speak English?); with a noun subject, some question words put the verb first: Onde fica a estação? (where is-located the station?).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

question.short: A question keeps a statement's order, and your voice rises: Você está pronto? A question word goes first: Onde está o carro?

ser-estar.name: ser and estar
ser-estar.about: Portuguese has two verbs for to be: ser for who or what someone or something is, estar for where a person or thing is and how they are: Ela é minha irmã (she is my sister), Ela está cansada (she is tired).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

ser-estar.short: ser says what something is (Isso é um livro); estar says where it is or how it is now (O livro está na mesa).

voce.name: você: you
voce.about: Brazilians say você for you, with the verb's ele form: Você fala inglês (you speaks English).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

voce.short: Brazilians say você for you, with the ele form of the verb: você toma, você está (you drinks, you is).

a-gente.name: a gente: we
a-gente.about: In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, a gente (the people) usually means we, with the verb's ele form: A gente vai (the people goes: we go).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

a-gente.short: In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, a gente (the people) usually means we, with the ele form: A gente vai (we go).

object-pronoun.name: Pronouns before the verb
object-pronoun.about: In Brazil, little words for me, you and each other (me, te, se) go before the verb: Eu te vi (I you saw).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

object-pronoun.short: In Brazil, me, te and se go before the verb: Eu te vi (I you saw: I saw you).

reflexive.name: Reflexive verbs
reflexive.about: Some verbs come with me, se or nos before the verb, pointing back to whoever does it: Eu me levanto (I myself raise: I get up).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

reflexive.short: Some verbs take me, se or nos before them, pointing back to whoever does it: Eu me levanto (I myself raise: I get up).

gostar-de.name: gostar de: liking
gostar-de.about: gostar takes de (of) before what you like: Eu gosto de café (I like of coffee).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

gostar-de.short: gostar takes de before what you like: Eu gosto de café (I like of coffee: I like coffee).

modal.name: Verb + infinitive
modal.about: After querer, poder, precisar and ter que, the next verb is in its basic form, the infinitive, with no word for to: Eu quero comer (I want eat).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

modal.short: After querer, poder and precisar the next verb stays in its basic form, with no word for to: Eu quero comer (I want eat).

ir-inf.name: ir + infinitive: going to
ir-inf.about: vou, vai, vamos and an infinitive say what's going to happen, with no word for to: Vou comer (I go eat).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

ir-inf.short: vou, vai or vamos and a verb's basic form say what's going to happen: Vou comer (I go eat: I'm going to eat).

progressive.name: estar + -ndo: right now
progressive.about: estar with a verb ending in -ando, -endo or -indo says what's happening right now: Estou comendo (I am eating).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

progressive.short: estar with a verb ending in -ando, -endo or -indo says what's happening right now: Estou comendo (I'm eating).

past.name: Simple past
past.about: One word with its own ending says what happened and is over: Eu comi (I ate), a gente comeu (the people ate: we ate).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

past.short: One word with its own ending says what happened and is over: Eu comi (I ate), ela comeu (she ate).

estar-com.name: estar com: I'm hungry
estar-com.about: Where English says I'm hungry, thirsty or sleepy, Portuguese says I am with: Estou com fome (I am with hunger).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

estar-com.short: Where English says I'm hungry or thirsty, Portuguese says I am with: Estou com fome (I am with hunger).

tem.name: tem: there is
tem.about: In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, tem (has) says both there is and there are: Tem pão (has bread: there's bread), where formal writing often uses há.

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

tem.short: In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, tem (has) says there is or there are: Tem pão (there's bread).

contraction.name: no, da, ao: a little word + the
contraction.about: em, de, a and por join the word for the after them: no centro (in-the center), da minha avó (of-the my grandma), ao cinema (to-the movies).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

contraction.short: em and de run into o and a after them: na mesa (on the table), no bolso (in the pocket), a chave do carro (the key of the car).

de.name: de: of
de.about: Portuguese joins nouns with de where English uses 's: o carro do meu pai (the car of-the my father).

source.note: First drafted by Lexicommons, open to correction. Short name and one-line rule added in revision 2.

de.short: Portuguese joins nouns with de where English uses 's: o livro da minha mãe (the book of the my mother: my mother's book).

demonstrative.name: esse, essa, isso: this and that
demonstrative.about: esse goes with an o word and essa with an a word, for this or that: esse livro, essa chave. On its own, isso points at a thing: O que é isso? (what is that?) Brazilians use esse for this as well as that; este and aquele are for when it matters which.

source.note: Added with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.short: esse goes with an o word and essa with an a word, for this or that: esse livro, essa chave. On its own, isso is that: O que é isso?

o-senhor.name: o senhor, a senhora: polite you
o-senhor.about: o senhor (to a man) and a senhora (to a woman) are the polite you, for someone older or someone you'd be formal with; their verb is ele's, as with você: O senhor sabe onde é? (the gentleman knows where it is?)

source.note: Added with the Portuguese lessons, open to correction.

o-senhor.short: o senhor (to a man) and a senhora (to a woman) are the polite you, with ele's verb, as with você: O senhor quer um café?

question-word.name: Who, what, where
question-word.about: quem, o que, onde and como ask for missing information: Quem está na porta? (who is at the door?), Como eu posso ajudar? (how I can help?). The subject need not move after the verb.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question-word.short: Use quem for who, o que for what, onde for where and como for how: Como eu posso ajudar? (how I can help?).

verb-preposition.name: A verb's partner
verb-preposition.about: Learn a verb with the words it takes: ajudar com o carro (help with the car), precisar de ajuda (need of help). The Portuguese partner need not match English.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

verb-preposition.short: Learn the verb with its partner: ajudar com o carro (help with the car). The preposition depends on the verb and its meaning.

time-telling.name: Saying the time
time-telling.about: For an event at two, say às duas or às duas horas (at the two hours). The number is feminine because hora is feminine; às joins a and as.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-telling.short: às duas or às duas horas means at two: Minha consulta é às duas (my appointment is at the two).

plural.name: More than one
plural.about: Portuguese nouns have plural forms; many add -s. Words that agree with the noun follow its number and gender: duas horas (two hours). Spoken agreement varies, but this path teaches the full agreeing forms.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

plural.short: Many nouns add -s for more than one: hora, horas (hour, hours). Keep agreeing words with them: duas horas (two hours).

conditional.name: Would like
conditional.about: The conditional can soften a request: Eu gostaria de marcar uma consulta (I would like of book an appointment). -ria forms also describe hypothetical results; they do not translate every English would.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

conditional.short: gostaria de makes a polite request: Eu gostaria de marcar uma consulta (I would like of book an appointment).

por-para.name: por and para
por-para.about: por can mark payment, a route or a reason; para can mark a recipient, destination or purpose. Compare pagar por seu café (pay for your coffee) and dinheiro para pagar (money for pay). Learn fixed combinations with their words.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

por-para.short: pagar por seu café is pay for your coffee; dinheiro para pagar is money to pay. Both por and para can translate English for.

infinitive-links.name: Linking an infinitive
infinitive-links.about: An infinitive can follow a modal directly or follow a linking word chosen by the expression. para gives a purpose: dinheiro para pagar (money for pay); gostar takes de: gostaria de tomar (would like of drink).

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

infinitive-links.short: para + a basic verb form can give a purpose: dinheiro para pagar (money for pay). Other expressions choose their own link.

imperative.name: Requests and instructions
imperative.about: For requests to você, this path uses forms such as ligue (call): Ligue para o médico (call to the doctor). Everyday Brazilian speech also uses forms such as liga with você; those are not inherently wrong.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.short: Ligue para o médico, por favor (call to the doctor, please): ligue asks someone to act. This path uses this você request form.

softening.name: Asking gently
softening.about: por favor (please) and a small request such as Você tem um minuto? (you have one minute?) can make an approach gentler. Their effect depends on tone and context, not a mechanical polite-word rule.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

softening.short: por favor can soften a request: Ligue para o médico, por favor (call to the doctor, please). Voice and context matter too.

ficar.name: Stay, be located, become
ficar.about: ficar takes different meanings from its context: Eu fico em casa (I stay at home), Minha casa fica na cidade (my house is located in the city). With a description it can also express becoming.

source.note: Written with the Brazilian Portuguese lessons 21–40, open to correction.

ficar.short: ficar can mean stay: Hoje à noite eu fico em casa (today at night I stay at home). Context tells you which meaning is intended.
